key_terms.meaning: The broad field of building machines that do tasks needing intelligence; rules may be hand-written.
Programs that get their rules from data instead of being told them by a programmer.
ML using networks with many stacked layers, so features are learned layer by layer.
Learning a map f: x → y from labelled pairs (x, y).
Finding structure (clusters, factors, density) in inputs x that carry no labels.
Low error on new, unseen data, not just on the training set.
Expected test error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise; simple models have high bias, complex ones high variance.
Output = 1 if Σ wᵢxᵢ ≥ θ, else 0; weights are fixed by hand.
The connection between two neurons; its strength wᵢ multiplies the incoming signal.
An MP neuron whose weights and threshold are learned from examples.
On a mistake: w ← w + η(y − ŷ)x, with η the learning rate; no change when correct.
Layers of units between input and output, each layer feeding the next, with non-linear activations.
One hidden layer with enough non-linear units can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region to any accuracy.
The non-linear function a = g(z) applied to a unit's weighted sum z.
g(z) = max(0, z); derivative is 1 for z > 0 and 0 for z < 0.
pₖ = e^{zₖ} / Σⱼ e^{zⱼ}; turns K scores into probabilities that sum to 1.
L = −Σₖ yₖ log pₖ; the standard loss for classification with softmax or sigmoid outputs.
L = (1/n)Σ(ŷᵢ − yᵢ)²; the standard loss for a real-valued target.
Computing a¹, a², …, output and loss from the input by moving left to right through the network.
Computing ∂L/∂w for every weight by applying the chain rule from the loss backwards to the inputs.

takeaways: AI, ML and DL are nested circles, and the innermost, DL, learns its own features from raw data.
Supervised learning needs labels; unsupervised learning works without them and looks for structure.
What matters is test error, and the gap to training error is read through bias, variance and noise.
An MP neuron is just a weighted sum plus a threshold, and it can already compute AND, OR and NOT.
The perceptron keeps the MP formula but learns the weights from its own mistakes.
One perceptron cannot solve XOR; stacking units with non-linear activations can represent any continuous function.
The activation's derivative decides how much gradient reaches earlier layers, which is why ReLU helps deep nets.
The output layer and loss must match the target: a number, a yes/no, or one of K classes.
Backpropagation is bookkeeping for the chain rule, not a separate learning theory.
bank_note: Long answers here usually ask for a full derivation (perceptron rule, backprop by chain rule) plus a judged comparison, such as when ReLU beats sigmoid or how you would diagnose an overfit model.

bank.q: Draw the nested circles of AI, machine learning and deep learning. Explain what changes about where the rules come from as you move inwards, using one Indian example at each level.
outline: AI: rules written by a human, e.g. a rule-based railway enquiry bot
ML: rules fitted from data, e.g. a model predicting train delay from past records
DL: features also learned, from raw text, image or audio
Each circle is a subset, not a replacement; DL is ML with deep networks

bank.q: Compare supervised and unsupervised learning. Give two examples of each from Indian daily life and state clearly what data each one needs.
outline: Supervised: labelled pairs (x, y), fits a map, e.g. UPI fraud yes/no, loan default prediction
Unsupervised: only x, finds clusters or low-dimensional structure, e.g. grouping customers by spending, compressing images
Loss functions differ: supervised compares with y, unsupervised measures reconstruction or density
Labels are the cost driver in supervised learning

bank.q: Explain generalization, overfitting and the bias-variance trade-off. Sketch how training and test error behave as model capacity grows.
outline: Training error falls monotonically with capacity
Test error is U-shaped: high bias at the left, high variance at the right
Decomposition: expected test error = bias² + variance + noise
Definition of overfitting as a large train-test gap
Remedies stated briefly: more data, regularization, cross-validation

bank.q: Write the McCulloch-Pitts neuron model. Show with chosen weights and threshold how a single unit computes AND, OR and NOT.
outline: Model: output 1 if Σ wᵢxᵢ ≥ θ else 0, binary inputs and outputs
NOT: w = (−1), θ = 0 for the single input
Weights are fixed by hand; this motivates learning in the perceptron

bank.q: State the universal approximation theorem and its conditions. Show why a single perceptron cannot compute XOR while a two-layer network can.
outline: Any continuous function on a compact set can be approximated to any accuracy by one hidden layer with enough non-linear units
Conditions: non-linear activation, enough hidden units, bounded input region
XOR truth table is not linearly separable
Two hidden units with step or ReLU activation, then a combining output unit
Statement is about existence, not about learnability or network size

bank.q: A perceptron with two inputs starts at w = (0, 0) and bias b = 0, learning rate η = 1. Apply the perceptron learning rule to the examples (1,1,+1), (1,0,−1), (0,1,−1) for one pass and show the weight after each step.
outline: State the rule w ← w + η(y − ŷ)x, change only on mistakes
Compute z = w·x + b, predict 1 if z ≥ 0
Step-by-step table of z, ŷ, update
Note the rule converges only if the data are linearly separable
Final weights give a separating line

bank.q: A network has 2 inputs, 2 sigmoid hidden units and 1 sigmoid output, with all weights and biases given. Compute the forward pass and then one backward pass to obtain ∂L/∂w for one hidden-to-output weight and one input-to-hidden weight, using L = ½(ŷ − y)².
outline: Forward: z¹ = W¹x + b¹, a¹ = σ(z¹), z² = W²a¹ + b², ŷ = σ(z²)
Output delta: δ² = (ŷ − y)σ′(z²)
Gradient: ∂L/∂W² = δ²a¹
Hidden delta: δ¹ = (W²)ᵗδ² ⊙ σ′(z¹)
Gradient: ∂L/∂W¹ = δ¹xᵗ
Numerical values through each step

bank.q: For each task, choose the output layer activation and the loss, and justify in one line: (a) predicting the price of a flat in rupees, (b) spam or not spam, (c) classifying a handwritten digit into 10 classes, (d) tagging a photo with several objects at once.
outline: (a) linear output, MSE
(b) one sigmoid unit, binary cross-entropy
(c) softmax over 10 units, categorical cross-entropy
(d) 4 or more independent sigmoid units, sum of binary cross-entropies
Rule: match the loss to the target's probability model, not to taste

bank.q: Write the derivative of sigmoid, tanh and ReLU. Using these, explain numerically why a 10-layer sigmoid network suffers a vanishing gradient while a ReLU network does not.
outline: tanh′(z) = 1 − tanh²(z) ≤ 1
ReLU′(z) = 1 for z > 0, 0 for z < 0
Gradient is a product of these factors down the stack; 0.25¹⁰ is tiny
Saturation of sigmoid and tanh pushes the product to zero; ReLU keeps factor 1 on the active side

bank.q: Derive ∂L/∂w for a weight deep inside a three-layer network, showing every use of the chain rule and naming each intermediate quantity.
outline: Write the loss as a composition of layer functions
Chain rule: ∂L/∂w = ∂L/∂a · ∂a/∂z · ∂z/∂w
∂z/∂w is the input to that unit
Define delta as the product of the first two factors
Show the recursion that carries delta backwards from the output
State the final matrix form of the gradient

bank.q: Analyse why depth is preferred over width in modern networks. Refer to representation power, parameter count and feature reuse, and give the limits of the universal approximation theorem as a design argument.
outline: Universal approximation says a wide enough shallow net can fit any continuous function
But the number of units may grow exponentially in input dimension
Depth composes features hierarchically, so some functions need far fewer units
Parameter and data efficiency, feature reuse across layers
Counterpoint: depth brings vanishing gradients, hence ReLU, better initialization, normalization

bank.q: A classifier gives 99% training accuracy and 62% test accuracy. Diagnose the problem with the bias-variance decomposition, then design a fix plan with at least four concrete remedies and say what each one targets.
outline: Large gap means high variance, not high bias
Confirm with a learning curve and k-fold cross-validation
Remedies: more or augmented data, L2 weight decay, dropout, early stopping, smaller network
Why each works: shrinks effective capacity or adds data
If test error plateaus, the residual may be noise or label error
Re-check after each change on held-out data only

bank.q: Evaluate the choice of activation function across the layers of a deep feed-forward network. Justify why ReLU replaced sigmoid in hidden layers and when you would still choose sigmoid or tanh.
outline: Sigmoid squashes to (0, 1), saturates, derivative at most 0.25, not zero-centred
Tanh is zero-centred but still saturates
ReLU: cheap, derivative exactly 1 for positive inputs, sparse activation
ReLU downside: dead units for always-negative pre-activations, hence leaky ReLU variants
Sigmoid stays in the output layer for binary problems, tanh in bounded outputs
Initialization and normalization must match the activation

bank.q: Backpropagation is often described as the whole of neural network learning. Examine this claim: show that backpropagation is only the chain rule for gradients, and discuss what else a complete learning system needs, including its failure modes.
outline: Backprop gives gradients only; it is not an optimizer
What else is needed: a loss, an optimizer such as gradient descent, initialization, learning rate schedule, regularization
Derivation sketch: delta recursion and weight gradient
Failure modes: vanishing and exploding gradients, saturation, bad local regions, dead ReLUs
Cost of backprop is about the same as one forward pass
Conclusion: necessary but not sufficient; the objective and data decide success

glossary.def: The long output fibre of a biological neuron that carries its spike to other neurons.
The branching input fibre of a neuron that receives signals from other neurons.
The cell body of a neuron, which sums incoming signals and decides whether to fire.
A short electrical pulse fired by a biological neuron when its input crosses a threshold.
The value a unit's weighted sum must reach for the unit to switch on.
A learned number that scales one input to a unit; the artificial version of synapse strength.
A learned constant added to the weighted sum, which shifts the decision boundary; also, in the bias-variance sense, error from an oversimple model.
A small positive number that sets the step size of each weight update.
One full pass of the learning algorithm over the entire training set.
The surface in input space where a classifier's output crosses its decision threshold.
A data set is linearly separable if one straight line, plane or hyperplane separates the classes exactly.
A layer of units between the input and the output layer whose values are not observed in the data.
The two-input exclusive-or function, which is not linearly separable and so defeats a single perceptron.
Repeatedly moving each parameter against its gradient: θ ← θ − η∇L(θ).
For composed functions, dL/dx = (dL/da)(da/dx); the rule that makes backpropagation possible.
The raw real-valued score z produced by a unit before the activation function is applied.
A vector of zeros with a single 1 at the index of the true class.
The state of sigmoid or tanh at large |z|, where the output flattens and the derivative goes to zero.
The shrinking of gradients as they are multiplied back through many layers, so early layers learn very slowly.
Splitting data into folds, training on all but one and testing on the held-out fold, then averaging, to estimate test error.
Any penalty or constraint that discourages complexity, such as an L2 penalty λΣw² on the weights.
A setting chosen before training, such as learning rate, number of layers or regularization strength.
The point where further training steps no longer meaningfully reduce the loss.
